title: Business Communication
tagline: Write, speak and listen clearly at work, with hands-on practice in every module
summary: Learn professional communication: choosing channels, writing clear emails, memos and reports, running meetings, giving feedback and working across cultures and remotely. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Communication basics
modules.summary: The communication loop, how to know your audience and how to choose the right channel.
modules.outcome: You can describe how messages succeed or fail, tailor a message to an audience and choose a channel on purpose.
modules.intro: Most workplace problems are communication problems in disguise. Missed deadlines, duplicated work and bruised feelings often begin with a message that was unclear, sent to the wrong person or sent through the wrong channel.

topics.title: How a message succeeds or fails
topics.html:
Definition

Communication. The process of sharing meaning so that the receiver understands what the sender intended. A message that was sent but not understood has not communicated.

Where messages go wrong
StageTypical failureFix
SenderUnclear about their own goalWrite the goal in one sentence first
MessageToo long, vague, jargonUse short sentences and plain words
ChannelWrong medium for the contentMatch channel to purpose
ReceiverDistracted, different backgroundCheck understanding
FeedbackNo one confirmsAsk for a reply or summary
Tip

Before you send anything, finish this sentence: 'After reading this, I want the person to ______.'

Consider how often a simple task goes wrong because of a gap at one stage. A manager writes 'please sort out the report', meaning check the figures, while the receiver understands it as fix the formatting. Both did their job; the message never carried the meaning. The cheapest fix is to ask for a short reply in the receiver's own words: 'Just to confirm, you want me to check the figures by Thursday?' That single line turns an assumption into an agreement.

Check what you just learned

1. Communication has succeeded when:
  • The message was sent
  • It was in writing
  • The message was long
  • The receiver understood the intended meaning (correct)

Understanding is the test.
keyPoints: Communication succeeds only when the receiver understands.
Failures can occur at any stage, so check for feedback.

topics.title: Know your audience
topics.html:
Good communicators begin with the reader, not with themselves. The same information is written differently for a CEO, a new colleague and a customer.

Audience questions
QuestionWhy it matters
What do they already know?Avoid explaining too much or too little
What do they care about?Lead with their interest, not yours
How much time do they have?Decide the length and detail
What do you want them to do?Make the action clear
What might they resist?Prepare for objections
Worked example

Same news, three readers

The server will be upgraded on Saturday night.

  1. To the technical team: the exact times, steps and rollback plan.
  2. To managers: the business impact and when services return.
  3. To customers: a short notice with the hours the service is unavailable.

Answer. Choose the detail that each person needs to act, not everything you know.

Common mistakes

  • Using internal jargon with outsiders.
  • Giving executives every detail instead of the decision needed.
  • Assuming that the reader remembers earlier conversations.

Check what you just learned

1. Which question should you ask first about a reader?
  • What do they already know and need? (correct)
  • What font do they like?
  • How old are they?
  • Where do they live?

It shapes content and detail.
keyPoints: Start from what the reader knows, wants and must do.
Different readers need different detail.

topics.title: Choosing a channel
topics.html:
Channels compared
ChannelBest forWeak for
EmailDecisions, formal requests, recordsQuick back-and-forth, emotional topics
ChatQuick questions, updatesComplex or sensitive matters; it gets lost
Phone or video callMisunderstandings, sensitive news, negotiationDetailed data; no record unless summarised
In personBuilding trust, difficult conversationsLarge amounts of detail
Shared documentPlans and collaborationUrgent notification

Rules of thumb

  1. The more sensitive the message, the more personal the channel.
  2. The more people need a record, the more written the channel.
  3. If a thread has gone back and forth more than three times, switch to a call.
  4. After a call, send a short written summary of what was agreed.
Watch out

Never deliver bad news or criticism only in writing if you can speak. Written words lose tone and are easily misread.

Check what you just learned

1. Telling someone their job is changing is best done:
  • By chat only
  • In a live conversation, followed by a written confirmation (correct)
  • By email only
  • In a group chat

Sensitive news needs a personal channel.

Key terms: flip and sort

Sender
The person who starts a message
Receiver
The person who gets it
Channel
The medium that carries it
Feedback
The response that shows understanding
Jargon
Specialist words outsiders do not know
keyPoints: Pick the channel for the purpose: record, speed or sensitivity.
Switch to a call when a thread goes in circles.

modules.title: Writing clear emails
modules.summary: Write emails that are read, understood and acted on.
modules.outcome: You can write a subject line, structure an email, rewrite wordy text and manage tone and etiquette.
modules.intro: Email is still the main written tool of work. A clear email saves a dozen follow-up messages; a vague one starts a chain of them.

topics.title: Structure of an effective email
topics.html:
The parts and what to do with them
PartGuidance
SubjectSpecific and short: 'Approval needed by Friday: Q3 budget'
GreetingUse the reader's name
OpeningState the purpose and the action in the first two lines
BodyOnly what the reader needs, in short paragraphs
ActionSay who should do what by when
ClosingCourteous, with your name and contact details
Worked example

Weak and strong subject lines

Email about next week's workshop.

  1. Weak: Hi
  2. Weak: Question
  3. Strong: Workshop on 12 March: please confirm attendance by Monday

Answer. A good subject lets the reader decide what to do before opening.

Style rules

  1. One main purpose per email.
  2. Keep paragraphs to three lines.
  3. Use bullet points for lists of three or more.
  4. Put the most important information first.
  5. Bold only what truly needs attention.
Tip

Read your email as if it were the only thing the reader would see today. Is the action clear?

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the best subject line?
  • Hi
  • Urgent!!!
  • Budget file: comments needed by Thursday (correct)
  • Question

It states the content and deadline.
keyPoints: Specific subject, purpose first, action with a date.
One purpose per email.

topics.title: Plain language and brevity
topics.html:
Short does not mean curt. Plain language respects the reader's time and reduces misunderstanding, especially for people reading in a second or third language.

Wordy to clear
WordyClear
At this point in timeNow
In the event thatIf
Due to the fact thatBecause
Please do not hesitate to contact mePlease contact me
I am writing to inform you that(Just say it)
It would be appreciated if you couldPlease
Try it yourself: Rewrite: I was just wondering if it might be possible for you to send me the report at some point soon.

Model answer. Please send me the report by Thursday.

Editing checklist

  • Delete filler openings.
  • Replace long words with short ones.
  • Prefer active voice: 'Meera approved the budget', not 'The budget was approved by Meera'.
  • Cut repeated points.
  • Check numbers, names and dates.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is clearer?
  • It would be appreciated if you could possibly send it
  • Sending would be nice
  • I was wondering about sending
  • Please send it by Friday (correct)

Direct and specific.
keyPoints: Replace wordy phrases and prefer active voice.
Be brief but not curt.

topics.title: Tone and etiquette
topics.html:
Without a voice or face, tone is carried only by word choice. Readers fill in the emotion, and under stress they often fill in the worst.

Tone choices
Instead ofTry
You failed to sendI have not received
As I said beforeTo recap
Why haven't you done this?Could you update me on this?
Obviously(Leave it out)

Etiquette

  • Use 'Reply all' only when everyone needs the answer.
  • Copy only those who need to act or know.
  • Do not write in capitals; it reads as shouting.
  • Check the attachment and the recipients before you press send.
  • Never write what you would not want forwarded.
  • Wait before replying when angry.
Watch out

An email is a permanent record and can be forwarded. Do not use email for gossip, complaints about colleagues or anything confidential unless the system is approved for it.

Check what you just learned

1. When angry about an email you should:
  • Wait and re-read before replying (correct)
  • Reply immediately
  • Reply all
  • Write in capitals

Time lowers heat.

Key terms: flip and sort

Subject line
The title of an email
Plain language
Clear, direct wording
Active voice
The doer comes first in the sentence
Reply all
Sending to every recipient
Tone
The attitude carried by words
keyPoints: Choose neutral, specific words.
Think before 'Reply all' and before sending in anger.

modules.title: Reports and documents
modules.summary: Write memos, reports and summaries that lead with the answer.
modules.outcome: You can structure a memo, write an executive summary and present data clearly in text and tables.
modules.intro: Workplace documents are read in a hurry by people who must decide something. Your job is to make the decision easy. That means answer first, evidence second, detail last.

topics.title: The pyramid: answer first
topics.html:
Many people write in the order they thought: background, process, findings, then conclusion. Readers want the reverse. Start with the conclusion, then support it.

A one-page memo
SectionContent
TitleStates the subject
RecommendationOne or two sentences
ReasonsThree or fewer, in order of strength
Next stepsActions, owners, dates
Tip

If the reader only reads the first paragraph, would they know what to do?

The pyramid works because it matches how senior readers behave. They scan the top, decide whether they agree, and read deeper only where they doubt you. If your reasons are strong and ordered, doubt is answered exactly where it arises. If you bury the answer at the end, the reader must hold every fact in mind while waiting to learn why it matters, and many will simply stop. Group your reasons so that each one is a single sentence that could stand as a heading, then place the evidence beneath it.

Worked example

Reordering a draft

Original: Last month we reviewed our printing costs. We collected data from all departments. Several options were examined. Our conclusion is that we should lease printers.

  1. Rewrite: We recommend leasing printers, which would save about 18% a year.
  2. Reason one: current repairs cost more than leasing.
  3. Reason two: leasing includes supplies and service.
  4. Detail: the department data sits in the appendix.

Answer. The reader now knows the answer in one sentence and can see why.

Check what you just learned

1. A memo should begin with:
  • Background history
  • The recommendation (correct)
  • Thanks
  • The appendix

Readers need the answer early.
keyPoints: Answer first, reasons next, detail last.
A memo has title, recommendation, reasons and next steps.

topics.title: Executive summaries and reports
topics.html:
Parts of a longer report
PartPurpose
Executive summaryA page that stands alone: problem, findings, recommendation
IntroductionPurpose and scope
FindingsEvidence in sections with clear headings
ConclusionsWhat the evidence means
RecommendationsWhat to do, by whom, by when
AppendicesDetail for the keen reader

Writing a good executive summary

  1. Write it last, after the report is done.
  2. State the problem in one sentence.
  3. State the key findings with numbers.
  4. State the recommendation and its cost or benefit.
  5. Keep it under one page.
Worked example

A strong finding

Weak: Sales fell. Strong: Sales fell 12% in the second quarter, from 4.2 million to 3.7 million, mostly in the north region.

  1. The strong version gives the size, the period and the place.
  2. It lets the reader judge importance.

Answer. Specific numbers beat adjectives.

Check what you just learned

1. An executive summary should be written:
  • First
  • Never
  • Last, once the report is complete (correct)
  • By someone else

You can summarise only what is done.
keyPoints: The executive summary should stand alone.
Use specific numbers and headings.

topics.title: Presenting data in writing
topics.html:
Numbers need context. Raw numbers in a paragraph are hard to digest; a small table or chart is easier.

When to use what
UseWhen
A sentenceOne or two numbers
A small tableSeveral numbers compared across a few items
A chartA trend over time or a comparison at a glance
An appendixLarge datasets

Good practice

  • Give each table and chart a clear title.
  • Label units (rupees, percent).
  • Say in the text what the reader should notice.
  • Round sensibly.
  • State the source and the date.
Watch out

Charts can mislead: a vertical axis that does not start at zero can exaggerate a small change. Show the whole scale or say clearly that it is truncated.

Check what you just learned

1. Why state the source of data?
  • To fill space
  • To look clever
  • It is a rule of grammar
  • So readers can trust and check it (correct)

Credibility.

Key terms: flip and sort

Memo
A short internal document
Executive summary
A stand-alone overview
Pyramid principle
Answer first, then support
Appendix
Supporting detail
keyPoints: Use a table or chart for several numbers; say what to notice.
Be honest with scales.

modules.title: Meetings and presenting
modules.summary: Plan and run useful meetings and give short, clear presentations.
modules.outcome: You can decide whether a meeting is needed, write an agenda, take minutes and structure a short talk.
modules.intro: Meetings are expensive: every person in the room is paid for the hour. A great meeting makes a decision or builds understanding that could not be done in writing. A poor one is simply a very costly way to read emails.

topics.title: Do you need a meeting?
topics.html:
What does your meeting cost?

Change the number of people, the average hourly cost and the length to see the cost of one meeting and a year of them.

Adjust People, Average hourly cost (rupees), Length (hours) and see Cost of one meeting, Cost over 48 weeks change.

Meet only when you need to

  • Make a decision that needs discussion.
  • Solve a problem that needs several perspectives.
  • Build trust or handle a sensitive matter.
  • Do not meet just to share information that could be an email.
Alternatives
Instead of a meetingTry
Status updatesA shared document or short written update
Collecting opinionsA quick poll or comments on a draft
Announcing newsAn email followed by a Q&A slot

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a good reason to hold a meeting?
  • Make a decision that needs discussion (correct)
  • Share a list of dates
  • Show you are busy
  • Read out an email

Discussion is the point.
keyPoints: Meetings are costly; hold one only to decide or solve together.
Information sharing belongs in writing.

topics.title: Agendas, roles and minutes
topics.html:
Before, during, after
StageWhat to do
BeforeSend an agenda with purpose, timings, owners and any reading, at least a day early
DuringStart on time, assign a timekeeper and a note taker, keep to the agenda, finish with actions
AfterSend minutes within 24 hours: decisions, actions, owners, dates
Worked example

Action items

Weak: Look into the budget. Strong: Neha will send the revised budget to Asha by Friday 14 March.

  1. Names the person.
  2. Names the deliverable.
  3. Names the date.

Answer. An action without an owner and date is a wish.

Common mistakes

  • No agenda, so the meeting wanders.
  • Inviting people who have no role.
  • Ending without recording decisions.
  • Letting one person talk for most of the time.
Tip

End with the question 'What did we decide, and who is doing what by when?'

Check what you just learned

1. A good action item has:
  • A vague idea
  • An owner, a task and a date (correct)
  • Only a task
  • Only a date

It makes follow-up easy.
keyPoints: Agenda before, decisions and actions after.
Every action has an owner and a date.

topics.title: Presenting clearly
topics.html:
Delivery tips

  • Know your first sentence by heart.
  • Speak slowly and pause after key points.
  • Look at people, not the screen.
  • Use few words on slides; talk to give the detail.
  • Practise out loud with a timer.
  • Expect questions and pause before answering.
Handling nerves
TechniqueHow it helps
Prepare and rehearseFamiliarity reduces fear
Breathe slowly before you startIt calms the body
Focus on helping the audienceIt moves attention away from yourself
Arrive early and test equipmentRemoves surprises
Watch out

Never read slides aloud. If your slides contain all your words, the audience can leave and read them.

Check what you just learned

1. A talk should close with:
  • An apology
  • A new topic
  • The action you want (correct)
  • Silence

End with what to do next.

Key terms: flip and sort

Agenda
The plan of a meeting
Minutes
A record of decisions and actions
Action item
A task with owner and date
Timekeeper
The person who watches the clock
keyPoints: Open with why, give one main point and close with the action.
Practise aloud; do not read slides.

modules.title: Difficult conversations and feedback
modules.summary: Speak up clearly and kindly, give feedback others can use and listen well.
modules.outcome: You can tell assertive from passive and aggressive speech, give feedback with SBI and listen actively.
modules.intro: Most people avoid difficult conversations until the problem is bigger. The skills in this module make them shorter, calmer and more productive.

topics.title: Assertive, passive and aggressive
topics.html:
Three styles
StyleSounds likeResult
PassiveWhatever you prefer... I do not mindNeeds go unmet; resentment builds
AggressiveYou always do this! It is your faultOthers become defensive or afraid
AssertiveI need X. Here is why. What do you think?Respect, clarity, solutions

Assertiveness means stating your needs and views directly while respecting the other person's. It is a skill, not a personality.

A simple assertive pattern

  1. Describe the facts: what happened.
  2. Say how it affects you or the work.
  3. State what you need.
  4. Ask for their view and listen.
Worked example

Saying no

A colleague asks you to take on a new task on a very busy day.

  1. Passive: Sure... (and you stay late).
  2. Aggressive: You must be joking!
  3. Assertive: I cannot take this on today as I am finishing the report. I can look at it on Tuesday morning. Would that work?

Answer. A clear no with an alternative protects relationships and quality.

Check what you just learned

1. Which reply is assertive?
  • Whatever you want
  • That is a stupid idea
  • You never help
  • I need the figures by noon. Can you send them? (correct)

It is direct and respectful.
keyPoints: Assertive means clear and respectful.
Describe facts, say the effect, state the need, listen.

topics.title: Giving feedback with SBI
topics.html:
Good and poor feedback
PoorGood (SBI)
You are carelessIn Tuesday's report (S) three figures did not match the source (B), so the client questioned our accuracy (I). Can we add a second check next time? (R)
You are rude in meetingsIn yesterday's meeting (S) you spoke over me three times (B); I lost my train of thought (I). Could we let each other finish? (R)

Principles

  • Be timely: soon after the event.
  • Describe behaviour, not character.
  • Be specific; use examples.
  • Balance honesty with kindness.
  • Invite the other person's view.
  • Give praise in the same way: specific and sincere.
Watch out

Avoid always and never. They are almost never true and make people defensive.

Check what you just learned

1. In SBI, 'B' stands for:
  • Behaviour (correct)
  • Blame
  • Boss
  • Benefit

What you saw and heard.
keyPoints: Situation, Behaviour, Impact, Request.
Describe behaviour, not character.

topics.title: Listening well
topics.html:
Listening is half of every conversation and most people are poor at it. They wait for their turn to speak.

Active listening
SkillExample
Give full attentionPut the phone away; face the speaker
ParaphraseSo you are saying the deadline is the main worry?
Ask open questionsWhat would a good outcome look like?
Notice feelingsIt sounds frustrating
Do not interruptLet them finish, then pause

Common mistakes

  • Offering advice before understanding.
  • Finishing people's sentences.
  • Looking at the screen.
  • Saying 'I know' when you do not.

Listening also means noticing what is not said. If a colleague agrees quickly but avoids eye contact or gives a short answer, there may be a concern they do not feel safe voicing. Invite it gently: 'You seem unsure about the timeline. What worries you?' People often volunteer the real objection when they are asked kindly and given a few seconds of silence to answer. Silence is not an awkward gap to fill; it is room for the other person to think.

Tip

Before you respond, repeat back what you heard. If they say 'Exactly', you can proceed. If not, you have saved a misunderstanding.

Check what you just learned

1. Paraphrasing helps because:
  • It wastes time
  • It confirms you understood (correct)
  • It avoids the topic
  • It is polite only

It checks understanding.

Key terms: flip and sort

Assertive
Clear and respectful
SBI
Situation, behaviour, impact
Active listening
Listening to understand
Paraphrase
Say it back in your own words
keyPoints: Pay full attention, paraphrase and ask open questions.
Understand before advising.

modules.title: Global and remote communication
modules.summary: Work with people in other places, cultures and time zones.
modules.outcome: You can communicate across cultures, run remote teams with clear agreements and handle written English for international readers.
modules.intro: More work now happens across distance. The same skills apply, but small differences in culture, language and time make mistakes more likely.

topics.title: Communicating across cultures
topics.html:
Cultures differ in how direct people are, how they treat hierarchy and time, and what silence means. These are tendencies, not rules. Treat each person as an individual and avoid stereotypes.

Dimensions to notice
DimensionOne endOther end
DirectnessSay exactly what you meanHint and imply
HierarchyTitles and seniority matterEveryone is on first names
TimeStrict schedulesFlexible, relationship first
ContextAll meaning in the wordsMuch meaning in the situation

Practical habits

  • Ask rather than assume.
  • Confirm understanding in writing.
  • Avoid idioms and jokes that rely on local culture.
  • Learn how to say names correctly.
  • Be curious about how others prefer to work.
Watch out

Avoid statements about 'how people from X behave'. Learn about the person, not a label.

Check what you just learned

1. A good way to avoid misunderstanding across cultures is:
  • Assume
  • Use slang
  • Confirm in writing (correct)
  • Speak louder

Check understanding.
keyPoints: Cultures vary in directness, hierarchy, time and context.
Ask, confirm and avoid idioms.

topics.title: Writing for international readers
topics.html:
Simplify for readers using English as another language
AvoidUse
Let us touch base offlineLet us talk later
It is a piece of cakeIt is easy
Ballpark figureApproximate figure
Drop the ballMiss a task
ASAPBy 3 pm on Friday

Guidelines

  • Short sentences, one idea each.
  • Common words over rare ones.
  • Write dates in an unambiguous form: 12 March 2026.
  • State the time zone with every time.
  • Use numbers and units clearly.
  • Avoid abbreviations unless defined.
Worked example

Dates

05/06/2026 is 5 June in some countries and 6 May in others.

  1. Write 5 June 2026.
  2. Add the time zone: 3 pm IST.

Answer. Clarity beats habit.

Check what you just learned

1. Which date format is least ambiguous?
  • 05/06/26
  • 26-5-6
  • 6/5/26
  • 5 June 2026 (correct)

Spell the month.
keyPoints: Use plain words, unambiguous dates and time zones.
Avoid idioms.

topics.title: Running a remote team
topics.html:
Foundations

  • Agree core hours when everyone is reachable.
  • Choose a channel for each purpose and write it down.
  • Set response-time expectations.
  • Write things down: decisions, plans, handovers.
  • Meet at times that rotate fairly across time zones.
  • Create space for informal chat.
Remote pitfalls
PitfallRemedy
People feel invisibleRegular one-to-ones and public thanks
Messages without contextInclude background and the ask
Always-on cultureRespect off-hours; schedule messages
Silence mistaken for agreementAsk each person directly
Tip

Write messages so they make sense to someone reading them tomorrow, without the conversation around them.

Check what you just learned

1. A good remote practice is:
  • Agreed core hours and response times (correct)
  • Always-on expectation
  • No documentation
  • One-way messages

Clarity reduces stress.

Key terms: flip and sort

Time zone
A region sharing one clock time
Core hours
Hours when everyone is reachable
Idiom
A phrase whose meaning is not literal
Asynchronous
Not at the same time
keyPoints: Agree channels, response times and core hours.
Write things down.
